english: a willing horse needs no spur
also: a fast-running horse needs no spurs

evidence: Cic. Phil. 3.19: sed tamen currentem, ut dīcitur, incitāvī (Lewis & Short s.v. incitō)
terms.comment: Literally “to urge on one who is already running”, of a person who needs no urging. Cicero marks it as a saying with ut dīcitur; so too currentem hortārī (Cic. Att. 5.9.1, Lewis & Short s.v. currō).

evidence: Plin. Ep. 1.8.1: addere calcāria sponte currentī (Lewis & Short s.v. calcar)
terms.comment: Literally “to put spurs to one who is running”.
Literally “a running horse needs no spurs”. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase. It is made from the classical saying.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency.
Cicero, Philippics 3.19, and Pliny, Epistulae 1.8.1, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (12 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
